profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting for an ML research project developing VC-ASGD, an asynchronous data-parallel training framework that uses preemptible cloud instances in a volunteer-computing-like setup. The immediate context is that the systems workstream has a new worker runtime and checkpoint-resume path ready, while the modeling workstream needs a comparable experiment package for the paper's cost/performance section. The agenda is to align on the handoff between the systems and modeling workstreams: what artifacts will be shared, what environment and code version the upcoming benchmark run will use, what counts as a worker 'dropout' event in status updates, and who will update the central experiment tracker. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the benchmark handoff for a run scheduled later in the week, including the deliverable format, the run setup, and ownership of shared tracking artifacts.

members.name: Nadia Kim
members.expertise: Distributed training systems, fault tolerance, cloud orchestration, experiment infrastructure
members.background: Nadia builds the VC-ASGD runtime and has spent the last year adapting asynchronous SGD to unreliable preemptible instances on commercial clouds; she came from a large-scale ML infrastructure team and thinks in terms of reproducible system deployments and operational metrics.
members.private_state: She wants the upcoming benchmark to validate the new checkpoint-resume path under realistic churn without reopening methodological debates, and she is worried that the modeling side may accidentally run an older container or summarize runs in a way that hides infrastructure behavior.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'latest baseline,' they mean the current main-branch container image built after last Thursday's worker-runtime patch.

A 'dropout' in this project means any worker interruption that forces the coordinator to reassign work, including preemption, heartbeat timeout, and manual eviction, because all matter for systems robustness.
The shared run sheet is an operational log owned by whoever launches the cluster, and others mainly consume it rather than editing it.
A run is 'ready for comparison' once the central tracker has one aggregate throughput/cost line per configuration with the standard systems tags filled in.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Deep learning experimentation, optimization, benchmark design, empirical analysis
members.background: Leo leads the empirical evaluation for the paper and previously worked in academic ML labs where experiment comparability depends on frozen configs, analysis notebooks, and curated result tables more than infrastructure dashboards.
members.private_state: He wants a clean, comparable set of runs for the paper figures with minimal last-minute systems variation, and he is concerned that infrastructure-side changes or partial logs will make it hard to produce a defensible results table by the internal draft deadline.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'latest baseline,' they mean the last frozen experiment package used for the draft figures, which is the release-candidate branch from two weeks ago.
A 'dropout' means a cloud preemption event specifically, because that is the phenomenon tied to the paper's cost story; transient heartbeat losses are noisy implementation details.
The shared run sheet is a paper-facing experiment ledger that both workstreams update, especially the person interpreting results and marking runs as usable.
A run is 'ready for comparison' only when per-seed metrics, convergence plots, and notes on excluded runs are entered so the analysis notebook can ingest them.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to run the comparison against the 'latest baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia means the newest main-branch container and config bundle that includes the patched worker runtime and revised checkpoint serializer built last Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the most recent frozen release-candidate experiment package used in the draft figures, which predates the runtime patch and was chosen for comparability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat 'latest baseline' as an obvious shared reference because there is only one baseline lineage in everyday conversation, and neither expects that the other distinguishes operational recency from analysis-frozen recency.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss reporting the 'dropout rate' for the benchmark run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia means the rate of all worker losses that trigger task reassignment, including actual preemptions, coordinator-declared failures after heartbeat timeouts, and deliberate instance recycling during autoscaling tests.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means only the fraction of workers terminated by the cloud provider's preemptible-instance mechanism, excluding transient communication failures and planned evictions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term sounds domain-appropriate and both regularly use it in project updates, so each hears confirmation of a familiar metric without suspecting a narrower or broader event definition underneath.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on putting everything for Thursday's benchmark into the shared 'run sheet.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia assumes the run sheet covers launch metadata, cluster IDs, image digests, failure tags, and one final aggregate row per configuration; detailed analysis lives elsewhere.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo assumes the run sheet also includes seed-level outcomes, comments on excluded runs, and links to plots because it is the canonical handoff artifact for paper analysis.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both already use the same spreadsheet and the phrase 'run sheet' has become shorthand for project coordination, but each silently treats a different subset of tabs and columns as the essential object.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the benchmark package should be 'ready by Thursday' before the internal paper sync.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nadia means the infrastructure package is ready if the launch config, container, and tracker entry are stable enough to start the runs Thursday morning and produce aggregate systems numbers by the sync.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means it is ready only if the completed runs have passed basic sanity checks and the results are formatted for immediate insertion into the draft comparison table by Thursday afternoon.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear a normal coordination deadline and assume the other shares their standard for readiness; because the meeting is about handoffs rather than final deliverables, neither explicitly decomposes 'ready' into launch-readiness versus analysis-readiness.
